item.title: Decision Models as Scalable Economic Surrogates that Capture Human Variation
item.description: arXiv:2611.05553v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decision Models (DMs), a new class of AI models, give fast responses and return a probability distribution over a fixed set of options. These properties make them candidate human surrogates in economic simulations and surveys, a role increasingly filled by Large Language Models (LLMs), which are costly at scale and under-represent the variation in human behaviour. We present a first evaluation of DMs as human surrogates in economics, comparing 10 DMs with 8 LLMs in three economic settings: a household spending survey on consumption, several classic economic games and a labour-market field experiment. Frontier DMs, those that score highest on general decision-making benchmarks, reproduce the variation in human responses more closely than LLMs in all three settings. They capture the modal human response as well as LLMs in the spending survey, but less well in the economic games. Frontier DMs are also roughly ten times faster than the fastest LLM and can be over a hundred times cheaper. Together, these results suggest that DMs capture the heterogeneity of human behaviour better than LLMs and make large-scale economic simulations more feasible.
item.dc:creator: Maxime Saxena, Fabio Caccioli, R. Maria del Rio-Chanona

item.title: Economic Policy Uncertainty Index for Poland: Data, Construction, and Validation
item.description: arXiv:2611.05640v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct a continuous monthly Economic Policy Uncertainty (EPU) index for Poland spanning January 2000 to June 2026, following the newspaper-based Baker-Bloom-Davis (BBD) methodology. The index uses six deep-history Polish newspapers (Rzeczpospolita, Parkiet, Gazeta Wyborcza, Dziennik Gazeta Prawna, Gazeta Polska Codziennie, and Puls Biznesu), scaled by article volume, standardized to unit standard deviation over a fixed 2000-2024 baseline (300 months), averaged across available papers each period, and normalized so the baseline mean equals 100. Because newspapers enter the panel at different dates, a naive expanding-panel average can jump at each entry point from a change in composition rather than real uncertainty. We correct for this using the BBD Appendix A splicing procedure: a backward chain-splice from the richest six-paper anchor panel that matches dispersion via a multiplicative scale factor and matches level via a multiplicative ratio over each overlap window, yielding an index that is level-continuous across all entry points. The index rises sharply during the COVID-19 lockdown, the 2022 energy crisis, and the 2023 change of government, with its largest reaction following the 2016 Brexit referendum -- an external event with major implications for Poland's economic-policy environment. In month-on-month changes, Poland's EPU is moderately correlated with the US (0.26) and global (0.25) EPU indices. Together with the event-based evidence, these modest correlations support our central finding: EPU Index PL captures economic policy uncertainty that is predominantly domestic, driven mainly by developments in Poland's own economic policy rather than merely international spillovers, though international shocks remain relevant insofar as they create uncertainty about Poland's own policy decisions.
item.dc:creator: Alina M. Landowska, Robert A. K{\l}opotek, He Zhang

item.title: The potential impact of fiscal rule changes on digital products trade
item.description: arXiv:2611.05714v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The WTO moratorium on customs duties on electronic transmissions lapsed in March 2026, allowing governments to impose tariffs on cross-border digital products, alongside other instruments such as digital services taxes (DSTs). Yet, how tariffs and DSTs compare in the revenue they raise and their effect on trade in digital products has not yet been assessed. Here we combine bilateral trade in 31 digital product categories in 2016-2024 with DST rates and tariffs on physical analogues, estimate gravity models and simulate alternative fiscal regimes. We find that digital trade is lower in destinations with a DST, but within destinations it declines only temporarily after adoption. In conditional scenarios for 2024 based on the event study estimate, adding tariff equivalents to DSTs raises revenue from USD 2.7 to 6.9 billion and lowers trade by about 1.4%, and replacing DSTs with tariff equivalents raises USD 4.3 billion. We also find that tariff-equivalent payments are attributed mainly to the United States and DST payments to subsidiary locations such as Ireland. In sum, these results suggest that tariffs on digital products could raise more revenue than DSTs at a modest cost in trade.
item.dc:creator: Sonja Mitikj, Viktor Stojkoski

item.title: Priced In or Bet On? Cram-School Lessons, Jeonse Leases, and Expected Appreciation in Seoul
item.description: arXiv:2611.05767v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: South Korean families spend heavily on hagwons, private cram schools that prepare students for the university entrance exam. This paper asks what access to them is worth in housing and whether the premium includes expected appreciation. Using 2,197,510 Seoul apartment sales and jeonse (lump-sum deposit lease) contracts from 2015 to 2026, located with a new business-address geocoder, the analysis compares flats within the same middle-school assignment zone and month. Flats near hagwons preparing high-school students for the exam sell and lease for more: moving from the median complex to the 97th percentile of such hagwons within 500 meters is associated with sale prices 11.8% and jeonse deposits 7.3% higher, or 5.6% and 5.9% with complex size held fixed. Hagwons teaching younger children add no sale premium once these are held fixed. A larger premium in deposits than in prices across complexes reflects convenience: buyers pay less than renters to live near shops and services, above all repair and personal services. For the same flat type, complex and month, hagwon access produces no detectable change in the jeonse-to-price ratio, although the test detects the reconstruction value of old buildings; nearby shops raise it. Hagwon access is thus capitalized in proportion into prices and deposits, as expected of a current-flow amenity without extra expected appreciation. New tenants pay no lasting premium over renewing tenants, and deposits did not respond to major education-policy announcements. The housing premium is a cost of the education race that measures of tutoring spending omit.
item.dc:creator: Samiha Tariq

item.title: Does Frontier AI Strengthen Cyber Defense? Evidence from Project Glasswing
item.description: arXiv:2611.06629v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Defenders and attackers race to find the same software flaws. I use the launch of Project Glasswing, which gave a small group of large US tech firms early access to Claude Mythos Preview, a model for finding software vulnerabilities, to study how access to frontier AI affects defenders, external researchers, and attackers. Using the universe of publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, I find that firms with access more than doubled their disclosures relative to Chinese and Russian tech firms without access, disclosed about 150 percent more high-impact vulnerabilities, and fixed reported flaws as quickly as before. As treated firms found more flaws themselves, external researchers, who sell their findings through bug bounties, reported about half as many vulnerabilities in treated firms' code and more in other firms' code, without leaving the market. There is no evidence that attackers exploited the additional vulnerabilities: the share exploited within a month of disclosure fell by about two thirds, mainly because a smaller share was already exploited when disclosed, while the number exploited did not change. Frontier AI helped defenders find and fix more flaws before attackers exploited them, but its restricted release creates an asymmetry in software security between firms in different countries.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Mosk

item.title: You Know What You Will Like: People Predict Their Own Ratings Better Than Recommender Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.06696v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recommender systems usually learn what people want from what they have done. Platforms could also ask people directly, but asking is costly: 98.8% of the prompts in our data went unanswered. Theories of statistical prediction imply that a person's own forecast adds little to a recommender algorithm built from many people's behavior. Theories of dispersed knowledge imply that people hold information about their own taste that the data lack. We test the two with the MovieLens Beliefs dataset. In 2023-2024, a homepage prompt asked members how they expected to rate movies they said they had not seen. Of 26,020 such expectations, 551 from 277 members were followed by a rating at least a day later. We compare each expectation with four benchmarks: the platform's own predicted rating, two collaborative-filtering models (matrix factorization and an item neighborhood), and a stack trained on other members' outcomes. The trained models use each member's latest ratings. People predict their own ratings more accurately than all four benchmarks (correlation 0.69, against 0.34 for MovieLens and 0.54 to 0.59 for the trained recommenders). Added to all the machine forecasts and features, the expectation lowers out-of-sample mean squared error by 26%. The gain holds when models are trained on earlier expectations and tested on later ones. A member's earlier expectations about other movies do not replace the current one. In ordering a member's own movies, the trained recommenders are statistically indistinguishable from the person. On old, heavily rated movies, the machines do as well or better. The results reconcile the two theories: the crowd's data suffice where they are rich, and the person adds information about the specific item. We derive four design principles for preference elicitation and recommender evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Zihan Chen, Lei Nico Zheng, Di Zhu

item.title: Dull, Dirty, Dangerous? Working Conditions and the Limits of Occupational AI Exposure
item.description: arXiv:2611.06888v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Automation is often justified as relief from dull, dirty, and dangerous work. I examine how these conditions relate to occupational AI exposure using 21 O*NET items across 754 US occupations. Higher exposure is associated with lower condition scores under a large language model (LLM) measure and AI Occupational Exposure (AIOE), with equal occupation weights and employment weights. Adjustment for physical demands, required education, training and experience, and wages reduces the composite association. The adjusted confidence intervals include zero for LLM exposure and remain below zero for AIOE. Separating repetition from restricted discretion also changes what the combined Dull score conveys. These comparisons show how item groupings and occupational characteristics shape the interpretation of exposure estimates. Occupational profiles offer a starting point for selecting contrasting research settings. Establishing desired automation or realized relief requires evidence about workers' preferences and specific interventions.
item.dc:creator: Siyi Yu

item.title: Pay and Beyond: The Evolving Rewards for AI Skills
item.description: arXiv:2507.20410v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This study examines the monetary and non-monetary rewards advertised in job vacancies requiring artificial intelligence skills in the U.S. labor market. Using approximately ten million online job vacancies posted between 2018 and 2025, we examine the development of AI demand, wage premia, and non-monetary benefits, including tuition assistance, paid leave, health and well-being programs, parental leave, inclusive workplace language, and remote work, across firms of different sizes. We find that demand for AI skills increased sharply following the introduction of generative AI in late 2022 across small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), large firms, and S&P 500 firms, while AI wage premia rose most strongly among SMEs. AI vacancies are significantly more likely than comparable non-AI roles to advertise non-monetary benefits, particularly remote work, inclusive culture, and parental leave. This premium is strongest among SMEs and large firms, but weaker among S&P 500 firms. Finally, we show that the relationship between wages and benefits shifted after the spread of generative AI: whereas complementarity between high wages and benefits was previously concentrated among S&P 500 firms, and substitution among SMEs, the difference across firm sizes has attenuated. Our findings indicate that the increased demand for AI skills has been accompanied by changes in compensation patterns beyond pay, as employers across the size distribution combine monetary and non-monetary rewards to recruit AI-skilled workers.
item.dc:creator: Alejandra Castaneda, Matthew Bone, Fabian Stephany

item.title: The Dynamic Theory of Economic Complexity
item.description: arXiv:2512.10672v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Why do some activities grow faster in some economies than others? We develop a dynamic model of economic complexity in which output is determined by a weak-link production function and investment contributes to the accumulation of capabilities shared across activities. We test the model empirically by exploring two of its predictions. First, the model predicts that the capability stock at which the accumulation of a capability is fastest increases with the capability requirements of an activity. This implies a transition from unconditional to conditional convergence and a tunable conditional convergence regime. Second, shared capabilities provide a mechanism for path-dependent diversification (the principle of relatedness), including signs for the expected interaction terms between relatedness and complexity terms in regressions exploring growth by economy and activity. We evaluate these predictions using international trade, and sub-national industry data from the United States and Brazil, finding empirical patterns that are broadly consistent with both. Together, these results provide a dynamical foundation for economic complexity theory and help explain how capability stocks and shared capabilities shape differences in the growth of activities across economies.
item.dc:creator: Cesar A. Hidalgo, Viktor Stojkoski

item.title: Computing Endogenous Transformations in Processing Networks: A Dynamic Calibration Approach
item.description: arXiv:2609.15452v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding how production networks endogenously transform requires a parametric model with non-neutral substitution elasticities. While the Cascaded CES (CCES) production function provides a rigorous framework, dynamically calibrating its structural parameters from time-series data constitutes a highly non-convex inverse optimization problem that typically falls prey to the curse of dimensionality. To overcome this limitation, we propose a structure-exploiting hybrid algorithm that leverages the physical upstreamness topology of the network. Applying this framework to U.S. time-series data, we calibrate an economy-wide multisector processing network and provide robust evidence that the empirical supply chain is structurally inelastic. Through Monte Carlo simulations, we reveal that this structural inelasticity acts as a macroeconomic impedance; it endogenously transforms symmetric microeconomic volatility into heavy-tailed asymmetric risks, causing a statistically significant mean sinking effect that structurally depresses expected aggregate productivity. %Ultimately, our framework bridges the critical gap between theoretical network non-linearities and empirical macroeconomic dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Satoshi Nakano, Kazuhiko Nishimura

item.title: Social Networks and the Propagation of Household Shocks to Asset Prices
item.description: arXiv:2611.01540v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When can local household disturbances move credit prices? I develop a financially weighted propagation operator on the social network. In a conditional household-intermediary equilibrium, its projection determines the household-demand component of the excess bond premium. Because responses decay at different rates across network patterns and channels, a location's relative financial importance generically changes with the horizon, so no single centrality measure summarizes exposure across horizons. Household measurements recover this projection exactly when they span independently measured demand sensitivities. Empirically, social exposure to storm-damaged counties is negatively associated with spending weeks later in counties outside the recorded footprints. In simulations on the observed network under the model's diffusion law, the operator predicts the propagated credit-premium component of held-out storms with about 30 percent less error than direct social exposure.
item.dc:creator: Faisal Quaiyyum

item.title: Stochastic Optimal Control with Measurable Coefficients and Applications
item.description: arXiv:2502.02352v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We consider fully non-linear stochastic optimal control problems with measurable coefficients and (local) uniformly elliptic diffusion. Using the theory of $L^p$-viscosity solutions, we show existence of an $L^p$-viscosity solution $v\in W_{\rm loc}^{2,p}$ of the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation, which, in turn, is also a strong solution (i.e. it satisfies the HJB equation pointwise a.e.). We are then led to prove verification theorems, providing necessary and sufficient conditions for optimality. These results allow us to construct optimal feedback controls and to characterize the value function as the unique $L^p$-viscosity solution of the HJB equation. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first results for fully non-linear stochastic optimal control problems with measurable coefficients. We use the theory developed to solve a stochastic optimal control problem arising in economics within the context of optimal advertising.
item.dc:creator: Filippo de Feo

item.title: A Financial Brain Scan of the LLM
item.description: arXiv:2508.21285v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We use sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to "brain scan" large language models, mapping internal activations to interpretable concepts and enabling targeted "steering" of specific features. We show that prompting models to adopt specific preferences activates many unintended concepts, complicating causal inference. In contrast, SAEs permit smooth, more isolated steering of target concepts. Furthermore, our scans reveal a stark disconnect between the model's internal feature contributions and its self-generated explanations, showing that these explanations are unreliable guides to its reasoning. Finally, SAEs provide a lightweight intervention for existing models, producing interpretable embeddings and allowing researchers to attenuate specific economic biases.
item.dc:creator: Hui Chen, Antoine Didisheim, Mo Pourmohammadi, Luciano Somoza, Hanqing Tian
